questions.q: State what a brute-force attack is.

markPoints.concept: trying every possible password until the right one is found
accept: every|all|all possible|one after|one by one|each one|repeatedly|again and again|thousands|millions|trial and error
markPoints.exemplar: Trying every possible password until the right one is found.

questions.example: Trying every possible combination of characters until the right password is found.
questions.paraphrase: Working through all the possible passwords one by one until one of them works.
questions.feedback: Every possibility, tried in turn. A dictionary attack is the same idea with a shortlist of likely passwords.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.4 Lesson 6 — Cracking lab, station 1: What is a brute-force attack?

questions.q: Which of these make a brute-force attack harder? Tick all that apply.
options: Using upper and lower case, digits and symbols
Locking the account after a number of failed attempts
Changing the font of the login page
correct: Using upper and lower case, digits and symbols
Locking the account after a number of failed attempts
questions.feedback: Length and variety increase how many guesses are needed; locking the account limits how fast they can be made.

questions.q: Explain why a longer password is so much harder to crack by brute force.

markPoints.concept: every extra character multiplies the number of possible passwords
accept: multipl|times|power|exponential|doubles|many more|far more|each extra|every extra|each character|per character
markPoints.exemplar: Every extra character multiplies the number of possible passwords.

markPoints.concept: so the number of combinations grows extremely quickly
markPoints.exemplar: So the number of combinations grows extremely quickly.

markPoints.concept: and the attack takes far longer, perhaps longer than is worth it
markPoints.exemplar: This means the attack would take years rather than minutes.

questions.example: Each extra character multiplies the number of possible passwords by the size of the character set, so the total number of combinations grows enormously with every character added. That means a brute-force attack would take years rather than minutes, which is long enough that nobody bothers.
questions.paraphrase: Adding a character multiplies the possibilities rather than adding to them, so the search space expands dramatically and the time required becomes so great that the attack is impractical.
questions.feedback: Three ideas: multiplication, growth, time. The third is what makes the password safe in practice.

questions.q: A password uses only the 26 lower-case letters and is 3 characters long. How many different passwords are possible?
questions.feedback: 26 × 26 × 26 = 17,576. Adding one more character would make it 456,976.
